title: Keep customers with no paid orders
prompt: Count October paid orders for every t1 customer, including customers with none.
hint: Put order filters in ON and count the nullable-side identity.

reasoning: The left input fixes the population at all tenant customers. Conditions on the optional orders remain in the match, so an unmatched customer is retained. Counting the non-null order identity then yields zero for that customer.

title: Find customers without a paid order
prompt: Return t1 customers with no paid order in the report interval.
hint: Use NOT EXISTS with the same status and time contract.
trap: No orders and only cancelled orders both qualify.
follow_up: Would a customer with a zero-value paid order qualify?
reasoning: The correlated subquery asks whether any eligible order exists for this customer. Its truth value is independent of how many items or payments the order has. A cancelled-only customer remains a no-paid-order customer.

title: Known billing versus complete billing
prompt: For customers with October paid orders, return known billed sum, missing bills and complete total.
hint: SUM ignores NULL; count missing observations separately.
trap: A known subtotal is not a complete total; all-missing SUM is NULL.
follow_up: What changes if the missing bill becomes an observed zero?
reasoning: The group contains actual paid orders, not preserved customer placeholder rows. Compare total order count with nonmissing bill count before publishing a complete sum. A known zero stays part of the observed data.

title: Enrich orders without multiplying billing
prompt: Return customer billing and item count while preserving job-level billing grain.
hint: Aggregate items to order grain before joining.
trap: A direct items join repeats the full billed amount once per line.
follow_up: Why is SUM(DISTINCT billed_cents) not a valid repair?
reasoning: item_counts has at most one row per order, so enrichment cannot multiply an order bill. Missing line evidence contributes zero item count, while the bill sum keeps its own missingness semantics. The result remains one row per customer.

title: Compare billing with confirmed payments
prompt: At order grain, show successful-payment count, confirmed amount and billing gap. Pending payments do not count.
hint: Reduce payments before enriching orders.
trap: An absent succeeded payment means no confirmed payment in this supplied complete ledger, not an unknown bill of zero.
follow_up: What new completeness evidence is needed for a partial payment extract?
reasoning: Only succeeded payment rows are reduced into settled. Joining that reduced table preserves each selected order once. The subtraction propagates an unknown bill instead of declaring an amount discrepancy of zero.

title: Category line totals
prompt: Sum line amounts by category for October paid orders, including item lines whose order bill is unresolved.
hint: Filter orders before aggregating line-level measures.
trap: Line totals are a separate source measure; they need not reconcile to incomplete or inconsistent order bills.
follow_up: Where would you investigate a difference between line and order totals?
reasoning: The measure belongs to item grain, so its sum is taken over item rows matched to eligible orders. This is deliberately different from summing repeated order bills. A category line may be known even when the order bill is not.

title: Customers who bought both categories
prompt: Find customers whose paid order items include books and software in the interval.
hint: Conditional aggregation avoids a multiplying double join.
trap: Repeated lines should not change category membership.
follow_up: How would you require all categories from a variable requested set?
reasoning: Each customer group is tested for membership of both requested categories. Several repeated books lines only keep the books flag true. No particular pair of item rows needs to be joined.

title: A NULL-safe exclusion list
prompt: Return t1 customers absent from exclusions, which deliberately contains a NULL.
hint: Use correlated NOT EXISTS.
trap: NOT IN with a NULL-bearing subquery can discard all otherwise eligible rows.
follow_up: How should an actual NULL customer identity be handled?
reasoning: The subquery checks an actual identity match, so a NULL exclusion is not equal to a valid customer ID. This avoids relying on NOT IN over an unknown comparison. Canonical customer identities cannot be NULL under the schema.

title: Top two complete revenue tiers with ties
prompt: Return customers in the two highest distinct complete billed-value tiers; retain ties.
hint: Aggregate and exclude incomplete totals, then DENSE_RANK.
trap: ROW_NUMBER caps rows rather than distinct value tiers; ranking partial bills can mislead.
follow_up: What would exactly two customers require?
reasoning: The grouped source first establishes complete known billing for each ranked customer. DENSE_RANK assigns the same tier to equal totals without leaving gaps. Filtering tiers outside the window-producing CTE preserves all boundary ties.

title: One deterministic latest order
prompt: Choose one latest October paid order per customer; equal timestamps choose the larger order ID.
hint: ROW_NUMBER needs a total ordering.
trap: MAX(timestamp) joined back can return several tied orders.
follow_up: How would the answer change if all latest ties were required?
reasoning: The first sort key finds recency and the second chooses one row among equal timestamps. The row number is calculated within each customer. The outer filter selects one record without throwing away that record original bill value.

title: Running known billing with completeness
prompt: For Oct 1-10, return known daily contribution, cumulative known contribution, cumulative missing bills and complete running bill when possible.
hint: Build a date spine and use explicit ROWS frames.
trap: Zero known contribution on a missing-bill day is not a known zero total; the completeness flag must remain visible.
follow_up: What does an unbounded frame start at after filtering?
reasoning: The date spine contributes rows for days with no orders. The running frame begins at the report start because this problem intentionally excludes earlier billing. Missing counts accumulate with known contribution, so a later row cannot imply complete billing after a missing input.

title: Seven calendar-day rolling bill
prompt: Show Oct 1-10 rolling known contribution and missing bills using six prior calendar days, including pre-report history.
hint: Densify days, calculate the window, then slice the output.
trap: Seven sparse sales rows are not seven calendar days; filtering early also loses lookback history.
follow_up: How would a seven-complete-day metric treat today?
reasoning: The source includes the history needed for the first requested day. The window sees one row per calendar day, then the outer SELECT limits presentation. Do not compare this result with a window built over sparse sale dates.

title: Month-over-month counts and a zero baseline
prompt: Return supplied paid-order counts for Aug, Sep and Oct, previous count and relative change; zero prior count is undefined.
hint: Use an explicit month spine and LAG.
trap: These supplied fixture counts do not establish complete real monthly reporting or a fair growth claim.
follow_up: Which maturity and as-of rules would you add to compare actual months?
reasoning: The month spine keeps the zero-order month in sequence. LAG reads the preceding count, not the preceding nonzero month. NULLIF makes a zero baseline undefined; partial real months would need a separate maturity policy.

title: Consecutive active-day islands
prompt: Return activity streaks of at least two consecutive UTC dates per customer. Count each date once.
hint: Deduplicate dates, subtract row number from date ordinal.
trap: Several events on one day must not extend a streak.
follow_up: What changes for local dates across daylight-saving boundaries?
reasoning: First remove repeated dates for each customer. Consecutive dates and their sequential row numbers increase together, leaving a constant island key. Grouping that key recovers a run without counting repeated actions as additional days.

title: Thirty-minute inactivity sessions
prompt: Sessionize c1 activity events. A gap strictly greater than 1,800 seconds starts a new session; exact 1,800 remains in the same session.
hint: LAG, boundary flag, cumulative SUM, then group.
trap: Use event time and a deterministic tie-breaker; duplicate delivery is not another user action.
follow_up: What if a late event bridges two existing sessions?
reasoning: LAG measures the gap to the immediately previous activity in event-time order. The first event and gaps above the stated threshold start sessions. A cumulative flag sum labels sessions before the final group counts their events.

title: Plan as of the order
prompt: Return the last plan effective at or before each paid order, with Unmapped when absent.
hint: Join eligible history, then ROW_NUMBER per order.
trap: Joining the current plan leaks future classification into past orders.
follow_up: What if history permits overlapping or equal-effective versions?
reasoning: Only historical changes effective by the order time are candidates. Descending effective time selects the last qualifying plan. The left join leaves one unmatched candidate when no history exists, preserving an Unmapped order.

title: Ordered onboarding funnel
prompt: For signups with seven elapsed days observed, count eligible users, first starts within seven days and completions at or after that first start but before signup+7 days.
hint: First reduce starts, then search for a completion no earlier than that start.
trap: A completion before the first start is not an ordered funnel success; the upper bound is exclusive.
follow_up: Would a different valid-attempt funnel need a different query?
reasoning: Eligibility is fixed before event matching. A first qualifying start is chosen per user, then only completions at or after that start and before the exclusive horizon count. This specified first-start model is not every possible multi-attempt funnel definition.

title: Exact day-one retention by cohort
prompt: Return signup-cohort D1 retention using a full UTC day window and only mature users.
hint: Use EXISTS so several return events do not multiply users.
trap: A cohort needs its entire qualifying day observed, not merely the start of that day.
follow_up: What is the policy for a signup timestamp outside midnight?
reasoning: EXISTS reduces any number of qualifying return events to one retained flag. The maturity condition observes the full day-one interval, including its exclusive upper endpoint. The final group compares users within the same signup cohort.

title: A late D7 event revises retention
prompt: Compute D7 retention at initial and later knowledge cutoffs while holding the event cutoff fixed.
hint: Cross two as-of settings with mature users; use a correlated EXISTS.

reasoning: The set of mature users and behavioral cutoff remain fixed. Each receipt cutoff changes only the event knowledge visible for the return test. The late consistent event therefore changes historical retention without implying later behavior in the old window.

title: Any return during days one through seven

reasoning: This return set spans seven daily buckets beginning one day after signup. A user returning on day two qualifies even without a day-seven event. Keep that bounded definition separate from exact-day and unbounded rolling retention.

title: DAU and seven-day active users
prompt: For Oct 11, count distinct activity users that day and across Oct 5-11.
hint: Count distinct customers over each interval, not sums of daily users.

reasoning: Both measures count customer identities, not deliveries or events. A customer active on several days still contributes once to the seven-day set. Do not sum daily distinct counts to obtain that larger interval count.

title: Repeat purchase among mature first purchasers
prompt: Find each customer first paid order across supplied history. Among first purchasers with seven days observed, count another paid order within that first seven-day interval.

reasoning: The first purchase is determined over all supplied paid history before the event cutoff, not only October orders. The maturity filter gives every selected first purchaser the opportunity to repeat. Another order at the identical first timestamp is excluded by the stated strict inequality.

title: Cart-level abandonment with a mature horizon
prompt: For carts with a full hour observed, count carts with a linked paid order in [created,created+1 hour), and abandoned carts.
hint: Use EXISTS over the explicit cart link.
trap: A later purchase does not satisfy a one-hour cart conversion; immature carts are excluded.

reasoning: The denominator is carts, so one customer can contribute more than one eligible cart. A paid order must reference the same cart and customer and fall inside its one-hour interval. The unfinished late cart is not labelled abandoned yet.

title: Segment activation by signup-time plan
prompt: Report the Q17 funnel by plan effective at signup, preserving an Unmapped segment.
hint: Reuse the same eligibility and ordered completion, then select historical dimension state.

reasoning: The funnel eligibility and completion rule stay unchanged when adding segmentation. Plan selection is anchored to signup rather than the current plan or eventual order. Missing history becomes its own visible segment instead of dropping users.

title: Exact repeats versus conflicting event identities

reasoning: Delivery count and distinct payload count answer different questions. Consistent repeated reports can collapse to one business event; conflicting identities require a correction or quarantine policy. Receipt identity alone does not resolve authoritative event truth.

title: Unknown and mismatched event ownership

reasoning: The initial identity-only left join makes both missing owners and wrong-tenant owners observable. The query is explicitly an ingestion administrator diagnostic over this fixture. A public application must derive and enforce its own trusted authorization scope.
